text.p: British companies are dipping their hands in their pockets to support charitable causes not only in a spirit of altruism, but to improve their image with consumers and boost sales, industry experts told Reuters recently.

They said the area of "cause-related marketing", where a company promotes its brand in conjunction with a good cause such as a charity, was growing fast as companies searched for new ways to win customers.

"Cause-related marketing...is an effective way of enhancing corporate image, differentiating products and increasing both sales and loyalty," said Marjorie Thompson, who was recently appointed by Saatchi & Saatchi ad agency to head its new cause-related marketing unit.
Saatchi & Saatchi Cause Connection is the first such dedicated unit at an ad agency in Britain. Its goal is to foster a closer working relationship between companies and charities.

Thompson, who takes up the role in September, does not have a typical background for an advertising executive. She was previously head of communications for the Commission for Racial Equality and a former head of CND, a nuclear disarmament group.
"Cause-related marketing is the ultimate in 'feel good marketing' and is something that consumers actually want," says Alan Bishop, chairman of Saatchi & Saatchi UK, which is owned by Cordiant Plc.
"We anticipate that it will be an area of huge growth and value to our clients," he told Reuters.

Research carried out recently among 450 major companies in Britain showed 70 percent of marketing directors and 59 percent of chief executives expected cause-related marketing to increase in importance over the next two to three years.

The research was done on behalf of Business in the Community (BITC), an organisation that promotes the involvement of companies in community affairs and whose members include British Telecommunications Plc, Cadbury Schweppes Plc and Unilever's Lever Brothers.
"Companies are looking at ways to invest in their corporate and brand reputation and cause-related marketing could be the solution," said Julia Cleverdon, chief executive of BITC.

"This research clearly shows that this is an untapped opportunity that could bring enormous benefits to the bottom line of both the business and the 'cause'. It's the ultimate win-win situation," she said.

Cause-related marketing can also save companies money, industry experts say. The rising costs of TV advertising and increasing fragmentation of media means companies are looking for new ways to reach consumers.

BITC said shoppers responded well to cause-related marketing and, when faced with competing consumer goods of comparable price and quality, would often opt for a company or brand that espoused a good cause.

It said 86 percent of consumers surveyed said they would be more likely to buy a product associated with a good cause and 64 percent said cause-related marketing should be a standard part of corporate business practice.
"Consumers want more sophisticated ways of contributing to causes that they care about than dropping some change in a collecting box," said Thompson.

Saatchi & Saatchi will initially talk to existing clients about matching them with a suitable charity and developing advertising campaigns, on-pack promotions or events. It will then seek new clients who may be interested in the concept.

Cause-related marketing on a big scale began in the United States. One of the earliest campaigns was run by American Express, which raised $1.7 million through credit card use towards the restoration of the Statue of Liberty.
A number of British companies have run cause-related campaigns, including Tesco Plc, the British supermarket chain, which started a "Computers for Schools" promotion six years ago.
Shoppers get points at Tesco stores that can be redeemed towards the purchase of a computer for a local school.
HP Foods has run an on-pack promotion whereby one penny is donated to NSPCC, a children's charity, every time a bottle of its "Daddies Sauce" ketchup is bought.

Saatchi & Saatchi said it would be looking for obvious fits between companies and charities such as a children's clothes retailer supporting a children's charity, but also for some less obvious links. "There is a lot of scope for creativity," said Thompson.

But she warned against what she called "tacky" fits between a company and charity. She said that if a credit card company, for example, were to donate money to a charity for the hungry every time credit cardholders used their credit cards in an expensive restaurant, it would not be a good fit and may offend some consumers.
"We have to ensure that any cause-related link does not damage the charity, so, for example, a health charity could not get involved with a tobacco company," she said.
"We also have to ensure that a company's reputation is not damaged by associating with a charity that has, for example, received some bad press about its financial situation."

BITC said companies and consumers considered school- and education-related the most important cause. Companies ranked the arts as the second most important, but consumers put the arts at the bottom of the list after causes related to the developping world, youth development and urban regeneration.
